claims.text: The initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles have a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
Femtosecond LSPR excitation deposits a large amount of energy into a nanoparticle lattice within picoseconds.
Ultrafast LSPR-induced heating drives rapid, non-equilibrium atomic diffusion in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles.
The laser-driven diffusion selectively reorders atoms at the nanoparticle surface.
Selective surface reordering creates a transient core-shell configuration enriched in high-surface-energy elements at the surface.
Elements with lower dissolution or reduction potentials migrate away from or deplete at the surface.
Elements with lower surface energies migrate away from the nanoparticle surface during ultrafast heating.
The high-surface-energy-enriched shell passivates the nanoparticle.
The reordered shell lowers the surface premelting threshold and the energy barrier for premelting relative to the nanoparticle core.
Surface reordering preserves the interior solid solution during premelting.
The proposed surface reordering assists consolidation of the solid solution during rapid cooling.
Femtosecond LSPR heating will produce early, surface-localized premelting manifested as a thin liquid-like shell.
Femtosecond LSPR heating will produce a measurable surface-to-core compositional gradient enriched in high-surface-energy elements.
Conventionally heated nanoparticles will melt more uniformly than nanoparticles heated by femtosecond LSPR excitation.
Conventional thermal heating will produce a greater tendency for nanoparticle coalescence than femtosecond LSPR heating.
Maintaining the nanoparticles in colloidal solution limits coalescence during heating.
The mechanism applies only when heating is rapid enough to prevent extensive diffusion beyond transient surface reordering.
